name: Yusuf Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, governments or political parties. We don’t sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage seven people who sort disputed delivery credits inside a large food distribution company, and after nine years I can usually get an ordinary week's claims closed without a drama. I'm 58, have a bachelor's degree, and I'm neither the branch genius nor the person learning the job; I like our paper exception book and have never used AI. My wife works at a pharmacy, our children have left home, and we send 400 a month to our adult son while he recovers from an injury. Between lower local management pay, the mortgage and that help, we've only 900 saved, and there are few similar jobs nearby; I'd like to finish at 66 but haven't confirmed the pension money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can get the credits right and let the clever announcements take a rest. A customer who's been charged for an empty pallet still wants the credit, not an explanation of how modern we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect my work to continue, but I'd still worry about the household money. My 2,800 take-home and my wife's 2,000 cover 4,700 in monthly costs, including annual bills, the mortgage and our son's 400, leaving only 100. Our 900 reserve wouldn't cover one month of full costs, and a repair could mean borrowing. The job being steady doesn't make the spare money larger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paper exception book and Friday claims check through the first year. Starting next month I'd cancel my 110 hobby-club membership and the 40 television package, leaving our son's agreed support unchanged for now. We'd put the freed 150 with the present 100 into savings, making 250 monthly only while both wages and other costs stayed the same. I'd tell my wife the actual balance rather than say we were fine and change the subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, with relief that the job itself isn't changing much. I'd miss the club, but I'd rather miss a meeting than hide a borrowing letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your son you were cancelling the club?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as a complaint or a bill he owes us later. We'd tell him what help we can sustain and review his needs together, without making recovery a deadline we invented to fix our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does saying you're fine matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife hears that as the bills being covered with room left over, while sometimes I only mean today's bills were paid. My wife deserves the account balance, not my proud version of it.

say: I'd focus on **correct credits** rather than modern-sounding announcements.
I'd remember that the **customer** wants the charge corrected, not a speech about our systems.
think: I expect **work to continue** but worry about a household budget with only 100 left monthly.
Our **900 reserve** is under one month's total costs, so a repair could still force borrowing.
do: Keep the **paper exception book** and Friday claims check through the first year.
Cancel **150 monthly** in club and television charges, leaving our son's agreed support unchanged for now.
Save **250 monthly** only while both wages and other costs hold, and share the actual balance with my wife.
feel: **Anxious about cash**, despite relief about continuing work.
S0.quote: My wife deserves the account balance, not my proud version of it.
fieldNote: His **baseline anxiety** comes from thin cash and an existing family commitment rather than an assumed AI-driven job loss.
The **250 saving** combines specified personal cuts with the current surplus and depends on both wages and other costs remaining unchanged.

steps.text: Continue the paper exception book and Friday claims check
Cancel the 110 club fee and 40 television package monthly
Save 250 monthly while both wages and other costs remain unchanged

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say writing credit notes, checking claims and planning the queue are exactly the work the company pays us for, so we deserve a direct staffing answer. I wouldn't tell the team my management chair was outside that calculation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own post could go because I check and allocate the same work the software is taking over. I've got experience, not some rare skill that makes the arithmetic stop at my door. With few similar local employers and little cash, I'd be frightened of losing the pay even if most people elsewhere still had jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the other four regional claims managers whether they wanted to join a written request for notice periods and access to internal vacancies before posts were cut. I'd draft it at home on my own time, include only colleagues who explicitly agreed and submit it only after they approved the final wording; we'd assume no employer agreement merely because we'd sent it. In the first year I'd keep doing the current claims work while employed and request written explanations of any compulsory system requirements, without claiming I could use AI. I'd make the same 150 personal spending cuts now and save 250 monthly while the household figures held.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a little less isolated if the other managers wanted to ask together. I don't need a grand campaign; I need an answer with our posts included.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you submit everybody's name if only two replied?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, silence isn't agreement, and being worried doesn't give me permission to speak for a colleague. I'd send it only in the names of people who approved the final text.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn AI if the written requirements demanded it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably put the paper down and hope another option appeared, which I know could make things worse. I haven't used AI, and asking for the rules isn't the same as having agreed to learn it.

say: I'd ask directly about **staffing** because writing, checking and queue planning are the department's paid work.
I'd include **my own post** rather than imply the manager's chair is protected.
think: My **post could go** because checking and allocating are exposed, despite my ordinary experience.
Few local employers and **thin cash** make personal wage loss frightening even if most people elsewhere retain work.
do: Ask **four managers** about a joint written notice/vacancy request, drafting in personal time and submitting only with explicit final-text consent.
Continue current **claims work** while employed and request compulsory system requirements without claiming AI competence.
Cut **150 monthly** in personal spending and save 250 only while household income and other costs hold.
feel: **Anxious but less isolated** if colleagues agree to ask together.
S1.quote: I've got experience, not some rare skill that makes the arithmetic stop at my door.
fieldNote: His **collective request** has individual and final-text consent gates and is not described as an agreement already won from the employer.
He admits **avoidance** of AI requirements without turning a request for written rules into completed learning or acceptance.

steps.text: Ask four managers to join a written request, submitting only with explicit final-text approval
Cancel 150 monthly in personal club and television charges
Save 250 monthly only while household income and other costs hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife the credit desk could be gone in 2028 even while somebody still unloads the lorries. I'd rather have that conversation before she sees me home at eleven on a working morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty and expect my wage to go around 2028, before robots in 2031. My wife's 2,000 leaves 2,700 of today's costs uncovered, and our 900 wouldn't fund even half a month of that gap. Her pharmacy work includes checking and answering that thinking AI can change too, so I can't call her wage safe until robots arrive. I'd be awake wondering which commitment I'd have to break first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our son and daughter for a family budget conversation now, including what our son's essential needs really cost, without assuming either child could give us money. I'd request actual pension access, net amounts and leaving terms while I was still employed, and apply for real local administration vacancies without pretending another thinking job was protected. I'd resign only for a signed offer leaving at least 2,800 take-home after extra travel, or a separately agreed funded household plan. In the first year after AGI, if my wage ended, I'd ask the mortgage lender about temporary relief and use a free community advice service for eligible support applications only after confirming no fee; no pension, award or support would enter the budget before entitlement and payment dates were confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, with a stomach that wouldn't settle at bedtime. I could write down the first calls, but I couldn't write down an income we'd already secured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop your son's 400 immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd explain that losing my wage changes what we can afford and ask what other confirmed help he has. We might have to reduce our payment, but I wouldn't announce a fixed new amount before understanding whether he could eat and pay his bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course that promised to rescue the wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without actual fees, hours and a real paid vacancy to compare it with, and I might still be slow to agree. We don't have spare cash for a hopeful certificate or permission to stop paying the mortgage while I study.

say: I'd tell my **wife** that the credit desk could go while lorries still need unloading.
I'd speak before a **job-loss surprise** rather than let her discover the situation from my unexpected arrival home.
think: At **sixty**, I expect wage loss before robots, leaving a 2,700 gap that 900 can't cover for half a month.
My wife's **pharmacy wage** also faces thinking-AI changes, and conflicting commitments would keep me awake.
do: Request a **family budget discussion** without assuming children's money, and obtain actual pension and leaving terms while paid.
Apply to **real vacancies**; resign only for signed terms netting 2,800 after travel or a separately agreed funded household plan.
Seek **mortgage relief** and eligible applications after wage loss through confirmed no-fee advice, counting income only after entitlement and payment dates.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, able to name calls but no secured replacement income.
S2.quote: We don't have spare cash for a hopeful certificate or permission to stop paying the mortgage while I study.
fieldNote: His **2,700 gap** uses stated total household costs and current pharmacy wages, with explicit risk to the other earner before robots.
His **family discussion** doesn't presume a cash transfer or abruptly remove his son's support before needs and alternatives are understood.

steps.text: Ask both grown children for a budget conversation without assuming financial help
Apply to vacancies; resign only with signed ≥2,800 net after travel or separately agreed funded budget
Request mortgage relief and eligible applications through confirmed no-fee community advice after wage loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to stop hiding the money problem inside the phrase nearly retired. I'd tell the family I wanted the figures for stopping, not a date copied from somebody else's leaving party.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 in 2031 and still expect my management work to go before the 2034 robots. That's closer to my hoped-for 66, but I don't know whether any pension could be paid at 63 or whether the amount would cover us. A few years to save matters, yet our son's needs and both wages could change before then. I'd be less caught off guard, not confident we'd already crossed the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get written pension payable ages, amounts after deductions and early-draw penalties now, and ask my wife to put her own figures beside mine. We'd keep the 150 personal cuts and save 250 monthly while both wages and other costs held, reviewing our son's support with him rather than assuming it automatically ended. I'd ask a no-fee community money adviser to compare the statements with our actual costs only after the appointment fee was confirmed as zero. In the first year after AGI I'd stop working voluntarily only if confirmed household income covered costs and unexpected bills, with any wait to a payable pension funded; otherwise I'd seek real paid vacancies and eligible support after job loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the wage ending, but more able to face an envelope while there's still a payday ahead. Nearly retired is a description of age, not an entry on the bank statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension statement gave an amount at 66 only?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what, if anything, was payable earlier and what the reduction would be, rather than assume three years could be filled with the same money. A pension projection at 66 doesn't pay a bill at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you call 250 a month enough preparation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it would be what we could put aside under this budget, not proof of retirement funding. If a wage or bill changed we'd redo it rather than multiply 250 by sixty and declare the family safe.

say: I'd stop using **nearly retired** to hide an unresolved money problem.
I'd seek our own **stopping figures** instead of copying somebody else's leaving age.
think: At **63**, I expect the job to go, but pension access and an affordable amount remain unconfirmed.
Saving time helps, yet **wages and family needs** can change before we bridge the gap to my hoped-for 66.
do: Obtain written **pension ages** and net amounts, including early-draw penalties, and compare both partners' figures.
Save **250 monthly** while wages and other costs hold; review our son's support together; book community advice only after confirming no fee.
Leave voluntarily only with **funded pension gaps** and confirmed income covering costs/contingencies; otherwise seek actual vacancies and eligible support after wage loss.
feel: **Alarmed but less surprised**, willing to open the figures before the paydays stop.
S3.quote: A pension projection at 66 doesn't pay a bill at 63.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **pension projections** at one age from money payable earlier and does not treat a saving multiplication as completed funding.
His **son's support** remains a reviewed household commitment, while voluntary departure requires both bridge cash and confirmed ongoing income.

steps.text: Save 250 monthly only while both wages and other costs hold
Request no-fee community comparison of both partners pension figures and household costs
Seek actual paid vacancies if confirmed retirement funding cannot cover the household

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the decade could let us finish our working lives in order if we deal with the papers now. I'd still warn my children that our possible timing tells them nothing about how their own careers will go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 in 2036, two years after the 66 I'd hoped to stop at, so the calendar is kinder. I still don't have confirmed pension income that covers our mortgage, living costs and any continuing help for our son. My wife's pharmacy income can change before the 2039 robots, so I wouldn't count ten more years of her pay. I'm less frightened by the date, but I can't call our living secure from age alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request written pension and survivor terms now and review actual income, mortgage costs and our son's support with my wife annually. I'd keep working while paid and healthy, using the 250 saving plan only while both wages and other costs held, without assuming ten more years of income. I'd choose a leaving date only after confirmed household income covered costs and unexpected bills and any gap to payable pensions was funded. In the first year after AGI we'd recheck the actual budget whether retired or not, seeking eligible support if needed and making no new promise to fund family expenses until we could afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious rather than alarmed, because there's time to find out whether 66 is possible. I'd like my last working day to be followed by an ordinary paid-for month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you bringing retirement forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, 66 was already the hope, and even that hasn't passed the income test. I'd rather move a date later than tell my wife a comfortable story and leave her with the missing money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son about help after you stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd discuss the actual amount we could afford against his needs and other confirmed income. I'd say no to an unaffordable new promise, rather than ask his sister to cover a payment she'd never agreed to.

say: I'd use the **decade** to put our own papers in order before finishing work.
I'd tell my **children** not to infer their career prospects from the possible timing of my retirement.
think: At **68**, timing follows my hoped-for 66, but I haven't confirmed pension income that covers the actual household commitments.
My wife's **pharmacy earnings** aren't guaranteed for ten years, so the kinder date doesn't establish secure living.
do: Review written **pension and survivor terms**, actual income, mortgage costs and our son's support annually with my wife.
Keep working while **paid and healthy**, saving 250 only while both wages and other costs hold.
Leave only with **funded gaps** and confirmed income covering costs and unexpected bills; reassess after AGI and seek eligible help as needed.
feel: **Anxious but less frightened**, seeing time to test whether stopping at 66 is affordable.
S4.quote: I'd like my last working day to be followed by an ordinary paid-for month.
fieldNote: The **later date** permits preparation without proving pension entitlement or advancing an existing retirement plan.
He keeps **family support** inside the affordability test and refuses to treat his daughter's unoffered money as a way to sustain promises.

steps.text: Continue paid work while healthy pending confirmed affordable retirement
Save 250 monthly only while both wages and other costs hold
Request eligible support if the actual post-AGI household budget needs it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be sixty and could lose the wage before there was any confirmed retirement income to replace it. I'd want written notice, the actual leaving calculation and somebody to help me establish what pension or support was really payable. I can keep the claims book balanced; I can't balance our house on a payment nobody has approved.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what helping family already costs before saying a parent ought to build savings faster. We chose to send our son money, and I don't regret feeding him while he gets well. I do regret saying we're fine so often that my wife has to guess which kind of fine I mean.

headlineQuote: I can keep the claims book balanced; I can't balance our house on a payment nobody has approved.
portrait: Yusuf is **58**, an experienced, average-skilled delivery-credit manager with a bachelor's degree and seven staff at a large distribution company.
He **never uses AI**, preferring the familiar paper exception book and direct conversations about disputed claims.
He and his **pharmacy-worker wife** have grown children, a mortgage and 900 saved while supporting an injured adult son.
His **family duty** shapes spending cuts and requests for help, while stopping at 66 remains dependent on unconfirmed pension income.
biggestWorry: I fear **AGI by 2028** most because wage loss at sixty could precede any confirmed retirement income.
whatWouldHelp: I need **written notice**, an actual leaving calculation and help establishing payable pension or support.
